dialog.r: unhõne pūchhā ki kyā āp riporṭ bhej saktī haĩ.
dialog.tr: He asked if you could send the report.

dialog.t: ठीक है, उन्हें बता दो कि मैं आज शाम भेज दूँगी।
dialog.r: ṭhīk hai, unhẽ batā do ki maĩ āj shām bhej dū̃gī.
dialog.tr: OK, let him know I'll send it this evening.

blocks.means: passing on what someone said, in your own words: “She said she was tired.”

blocks.p: **Said that.** To pass on what someone said, join it with {{कि|ki}} “that”: {{उसने कहा कि…|usne kahā ki…}} “he said that…”. Then Hindi simply repeats what was said, **in the speaker's own tense**. Rahul said {{मैं कल नहीं आ पाऊँगा|maĩ kal nahī̃ ā pāū̃gā}} “I won't be able to come tomorrow”, and you report {{राहुल ने कहा कि वह कल नहीं आ पाएगा|rāhul ne kahā ki vah kal nahī̃ ā pāegā}}. Only the person changes ({{मैं|maĩ}} → {{वह|vah}}); his future stays the future. English shifts it back (“he said he *wouldn't*”); Hindi doesn't.

**Say, tell, ask.** {{कहना|kahnā}} “to say”, {{बताना|batānā}} “to tell, let know” and {{पूछना|pūchhnā}} “to ask” all take {{ने|ne}} in the past (lesson 27). The person you tell takes {{को|ko}} with {{बताना|batānā}} ({{उसने मुझे बताया|usne mujhe batāyā}} “he told me”) but {{से|se}} with {{कहना|kahnā}} and {{पूछना|pūchhnā}} ({{उसने मुझसे पूछा|usne mujhse pūchhā}} “he asked me”).

table: {{उसने कहा कि वह थकी हुई है।|usne kahā ki vah thakī huī hai.}}
{{उसने मुझे बताया कि वह भारत जा रहा है।|usne mujhe batāyā ki vah bhārat jā rahā hai.}}
He told me he was going to India.
{{उसने पूछा कि क्या मैं आऊँगा।|usne pūchhā ki kyā maĩ āū̃gā.}}
{{उसने पूछा कि स्टेशन कहाँ है।|usne pūchhā ki sṭeshan kahā̃ hai.}}
She asked where the station was.

blocks.p: **Asking.** A reported yes-or-no question keeps its {{क्या|kyā}} after {{कि|ki}}: {{उन्होंने पूछा कि क्या आप रिपोर्ट भेज सकती हैं|unhõne pūchhā ki kyā āp riporṭ bhej saktī haĩ}}. A question with a question word just keeps it: {{… कि स्टेशन कहाँ है|… ki sṭeshan kahā̃ hai}}. The word order doesn't change.

ex.t: उसने कहा कि वह कल आएगा।
ex.r: usne kahā ki vah kal āegā.
ex.tr: He said he would come tomorrow.

ex.t: माँ ने कहा कि खाना तैयार है।
ex.r: mā̃ ne kahā ki khānā taiyār hai.

ex.t: प्रिया ने मुझे बताया कि वह दिल्ली जा रही है।
ex.r: priyā ne mujhe batāyā ki vah dillī jā rahī hai.
ex.tr: Priya told me she was going to Delhi.

ex.t: उन्होंने पूछा कि क्या हमें मदद चाहिए।
ex.r: unhõne pūchhā ki kyā hamẽ madad chāhie.

blocks.p: **Want someone to.** English says “I want *you to* come”; Hindi says “I want *that* you come”, with the subjunctive (lesson 24): {{मैं चाहता हूँ कि तुम आओ|maĩ chāhtā hū̃ ki tum āo}}. The subjunctive is the future without its {{-गा|-gā}}: {{मैं आऊँ|maĩ āū̃}}, {{वह आए|vah āe}}, {{तुम आओ|tum āo}}, {{आप आएँ|āp āẽ}}, {{हम आएँ|ham āẽ}}.

**Telling someone to.** {{कहना कि|kahnā ki}} + the subjunctive is “to tell someone to”: {{उन्होंने कहा कि तुम उन्हें ले आओ|unhõne kahā ki tum unhẽ le āo}} “She asked you to pick her up”. Compare {{उसने कहा कि वह आएगा|usne kahā ki vah āegā}} “he said he *would* come” (a fact: the future, lesson 41) with {{उसने कहा कि मैं आऊँ|usne kahā ki maĩ āū̃}} “he told me to come” (a wish: the subjunctive).

**So that.** {{ताकि|tāki}} “so that” takes the subjunctive too: {{मैं जल्दी निकलूँगा ताकि ट्रेन न छूटे|maĩ jaldī niklū̃gā tāki ṭren na chhūṭe}} “I'll leave early so that I don't miss the train”. With the subjunctive, “not” is usually {{न|na}}.

lessons.summary: Make plans that depend on something: “If it rains, we'll stay home”, “Hurry up, or we'll be late.”
lessons.topic: {{अगर … तो|agar … to}} “if … then”, with the past, the subjunctive or the future after {{अगर|agar}}; {{नहीं तो|nahī̃ to}} “otherwise”

blocks.p: **If … then.** {{अगर|agar}} “if” starts the condition and {{तो|to}} “then” starts the result: {{अगर समय मिला, तो मैं आऊँगी|agar samay milā, to maĩ āū̃gī}} “If I get time, I'll come”. Hindi keeps {{तो|to}} even where English leaves “then” out.

**Which form after {{अगर|agar}}?** Three are used, with little difference: the future ({{अगर बारिश होगी|agar bārish hogī}}), the subjunctive ({{अगर बारिश हो|agar bārish ho}}), or, very often in speech, the simple past ({{अगर बारिश हुई|agar bārish huī}}), as if it had already happened. The result is usually the future or a command.

table: {{अगर बारिश हुई, तो हम नहीं जाएँगे।|agar bārish huī, to ham nahī̃ jāẽge.}}

{{अगर आप चाहें, तो मैं आपकी मदद करूँ?|agar āp chāhẽ, to maĩ āpkī madad karū̃?}}
If you like, shall I help you?
{{अगर तुम आओगे, तो मज़ा आएगा।|agar tum āoge, to mazā āegā.}}
If you come, it'll be fun.

blocks.p: **What's always true** takes the present on both sides: {{अगर मैं कॉफ़ी पीता हूँ, तो मुझे नींद नहीं आती|agar maĩ kôfī pītā hū̃, to mujhe nīnd nahī̃ ātī}} “If I drink coffee, I can't sleep”. And {{नहीं तो|nahī̃ to}} is “otherwise, or else”: {{जल्दी करो, नहीं तो देर हो जाएगी|jaldī karo, nahī̃ to der ho jāegī}} “Hurry up, or we'll be late”.

lessons.title: Say which one you mean
lessons.summary: Point people and things out by what they do: “The girl in the red sari is my sister”, “the hotel we stayed in”.
lessons.topic: {{जो … वह|jo … vah}} “who, which … that one”; {{जिस|jis}}, {{जिन|jin}} before a postposition; {{जिसने|jisne}}; {{जो भी|jo bhī}} “whatever”

goal.t: जो लड़की लाल साड़ी में है, वह मेरी बहन है।
goal.r: jo laṛkī lāl sāṛī mẽ hai, vah merī bahan hai.
goal.tr: The girl in the red sari is my sister.

dialog.t: वह आदमी कौन है जो सबके साथ नाच रहा है?
dialog.r: vah ādmī kaun hai jo sabke sāth nāch rahā hai?
dialog.tr: Who's that man who's dancing with everyone?

dialog.t: वह मेरे चाचा हैं। और जो औरत उनके साथ है, वह मेरी चाची हैं।
dialog.r: vah mere chāchā haĩ. aur jo aurat unke sāth hai, vah merī chāchī haĩ.
dialog.tr: That's my uncle. And the woman who's with him is my aunt.

dialog.t: और जिस लड़के ने मुझे पानी दिया, वह कौन था?
dialog.r: aur jis laṛke ne mujhe pānī diyā, vah kaun thā?
dialog.tr: And the boy who gave me water, who was he?

dialog.t: वह मेरा चचेरा भाई है। जो भी चाहिए, उससे माँग लो!
dialog.r: vah merā chacherā bhāī hai. jo bhī chāhie, usse māṅg lo!
dialog.tr: That's my cousin. Whatever you need, just ask him!

blocks.means: a part of a sentence that says which person or thing you mean: “the girl *who is in the red sari*”.

blocks.p: **The one who.** English puts “who” after the noun (“the girl *who*…”). Hindi uses a pair: {{जो|jo}} “who, which” in the first half, and {{वह|vah}} “that one” to start the second: {{जो लड़की लाल साड़ी में है, वह मेरी बहन है|jo laṛkī lāl sāṛī mẽ hai, vah merī bahan hai}}, word for word “which girl is in the red sari, she is my sister”. For more than one, {{वे|ve}}: {{जो लोग…, वे…|jo log…, ve…}}.

**Before a postposition, or with {{ने|ne}},** {{जो|jo}} becomes {{जिस|jis}} (one) or {{जिन|jin}} (more than one), just as {{वह|vah}} becomes {{उस|us}} (lesson 9): {{जिस होटल में हम रुके, वह बहुत अच्छा था|jis hoṭal mẽ ham ruke, vah bahut achchhā thā}} “The hotel we stayed in was very nice”. With {{ने|ne}}: {{जिसने|jisne}}, {{जिन्होंने|jinhõne}}.

table: {{जो किताब मेज़ पर है, वह मेरी है।|jo kitāb mez par hai, vah merī hai.}} The book on the table is mine.
{{जिस घर में मैं रहता हूँ, वह पुराना है।|jis ghar mẽ maĩ rahtā hū̃, vah purānā hai.}} The house I live in is old.
{{जिसने फ़ोन किया, वह कौन था?|jisne fon kiyā, vah kaun thā?}} Who was it that called?
{{जो भी चाहिए, ले लो।|jo bhī chāhie, le lo.}} Take whatever you need.

blocks.p: **After the noun, too.** In speech, the {{जो|jo}} part can also come after the noun, as in English: {{वह आदमी कौन है जो नाच रहा है?|vah ādmī kaun hai jo nāch rahā hai?}} “Who's the man who's dancing?”

ex.t: जिस लड़की से मैं कल मिला, वह डॉक्टर है।
ex.r: jis laṛkī se maĩ kal milā, vah ḍôkṭar hai.
ex.tr: The girl I met yesterday is a doctor.

ex.t: जो लोग यहाँ रहते हैं, वे बहुत अच्छे हैं।
ex.r: jo log yahā̃ rahte haĩ, ve bahut achchhe haĩ.
ex.tr: The people who live here are very nice.

ex.t: जिसने यह खाना बनाया, उसे बधाई!
ex.r: jisne yah khānā banāyā, use badhāī!

ex.r: mujhe vah film bahut pasand āī jo hamne kal dekhī.
ex.tr: I really liked the movie we saw yesterday.
ex.note: here the {{जो|jo}} part comes after; {{पसंद आना|pasand ānā}} is “to like (something you've just seen or tried)”

ex.t: जिस दुकान पर मैं काम करती हूँ, वह स्टेशन के पास है।
ex.r: jis dukān par maĩ kām kartī hū̃, vah sṭeshan ke pās hai.
ex.tr: The shop I work at is near the station.

mistakes.wrong: जो होटल में हम रुके, वह अच्छा था।

mistakes.right: जिसने यह बनाया, वह बहुत होशियार है।
mistakes.tr: Whoever made this is very clever.
mistakes.why: A transitive verb in the past: {{जिसने|jisne}}.

lessons.title: Say when, where and as soon as
lessons.summary: Join ideas in time and place: “When you come, we'll talk”, “Wherever you go…”, “as soon as”, “until”.
lessons.topic: {{जब … तब|jab … tab}}, {{जहाँ … वहाँ|jahā̃ … vahā̃}}, {{जैसे ही|jaise hī}} “as soon as”, {{जब तक|jab tak}} “as long as”, {{जब तक … न|jab tak … na}} “until”

goal.t: जब तुम आओगे, तब बात करेंगे।
goal.r: jab tum āoge, tab bāt karẽge.
goal.tr: When you come, we'll talk.

dialog.t: जैसे ही तुम पहुँचो, मुझे मैसेज करना।
dialog.r: jaise hī tum pahũcho, mujhe maisej karnā.
dialog.tr: As soon as you arrive, text me.

dialog.t: ठीक है। और जब तक मैं न आऊँ, तुम खाना मत खाना!
dialog.r: ṭhīk hai. aur jab tak maĩ na āū̃, tum khānā mat khānā!
dialog.tr: OK. And don't eat until I get there!

dialog.t: हा हा, ठीक है। जहाँ हम पिछली बार मिले थे, वहीं मिलें?
dialog.r: hā hā, ṭhīk hai. jahā̃ ham pichhlī bār mile the, vahī̃ milẽ?
dialog.tr: Ha ha, OK. Shall we meet where we met last time?

dialog.r: hā̃, vahī̃.
dialog.tr: Yes, right there.

blocks.p: **When … then.** Like {{जो … वह|jo … vah}} (lesson 44), Hindi joins time with a pair: {{जब|jab}} “when” … {{तब|tab}} “then”. {{तब|tab}} can be left out, as in {{जब मैं छोटा था, …|jab maĩ chhoṭā thā, …}} (lesson 31). For the future, Hindi says “when you *will* come”: {{जब तुम आओगे, तब बात करेंगे|jab tum āoge, tab bāt karẽge}}.

**Where … there.** {{जहाँ|jahā̃}} “where” … {{वहाँ|vahā̃}} “there”: {{जहाँ हम रहते हैं, वहाँ बहुत पेड़ हैं|jahā̃ ham rahte haĩ, vahā̃ bahut peṛ haĩ}} “Where we live, there are lots of trees”. {{वहीं|vahī̃}} is “right there”, and {{जब भी|jab bhī}}, {{जहाँ भी|jahā̃ bhī}} are “whenever”, “wherever”.

table: {{जब मैं पहुँचा, तब वह सो रहा था।|jab maĩ pahũchā, tab vah so rahā thā.}}
When I arrived, he was asleep.
{{जहाँ तुम जाओगे, वहाँ मैं भी जाऊँगा।|jahā̃ tum jāoge, vahā̃ maĩ bhī jāū̃gā.}}
Wherever you go, I'll go too.
{{जैसे ही वह आया, बारिश शुरू हो गई।|jaise hī vah āyā, bārish shurū ho gaī.}}
As soon as he came, it started to rain.
{{जब तक तुम यहाँ हो, मैं भी रुकूँगी।|jab tak tum yahā̃ ho, maĩ bhī rukū̃gī.}}
As long as you're here, I'll stay too.

blocks.p: **Until.** {{जब तक|jab tak}} is “as long as”; with {{न|na}} or {{नहीं|nahī̃}} it becomes “until”: {{जब तक मैं न आऊँ, खाना मत खाना|jab tak maĩ na āū̃, khānā mat khānā}} “Don't eat until I come”, word for word “as long as I don't come, don't eat”. With a noun, “until” is just {{तक|tak}}: {{पाँच बजे तक|pā̃ch baje tak}} (lesson 18).

ex.t: जब मैं घर पहुँचा, सब सो रहे थे।
ex.r: jab maĩ ghar pahũchā, sab so rahe the.
ex.tr: When I got home, everyone was asleep.

ex.r: jaise hī film khatm huī, ham ghar chale gae.

ex.t: जब तक बारिश नहीं रुकती, हम यहीं रहेंगे।
ex.r: jab tak bārish nahī̃ ruktī, ham yahī̃ rahẽge.
ex.tr: We'll stay here until the rain stops.

ex.t: जब भी मैं दिल्ली जाता हूँ, उनसे मिलता हूँ।
